The DOORS are attested reading-traditions surfaced from the retrieved reception store (~/reception-corpus), NOT authored from recall; every witness `reading` is the source's own words, lightly trimmed (Glossa italic lemma markers dropped). The editorial framing (trap/hinge/gravity/synthesis/claim/say/do/subtract) is AI-drafted and pending Wilson's curation. [Authored 2026-10-06, Opus, Phase 4b brief, born v2: Gospel doors from the Catena Aurea (Newman tr.) rows on Matt 22:34-46 (Augustine, Pseudo-Chrysostom, Jerome, Origen) plus Glossa ordinaria (Migne) 22:37 and 22:44, Wesley's Notes 22:43-44, and the Catena intertext notes on Lev 19:18 and Ps 110:1; both tracks authored from src/turn_pull.py output plus direct Catena-intertext rows from the reception store. Semicontinuous: three Deuteronomy 34 doors (Wesley 34:1/34:4/34:5/34:8/34:12, Migne 34:1/34:8/34:10, Catena intertext at 1 Cor 13:8-12). Complementary: three Leviticus 19 doors (Wesley 19:2/19:15/19:17/19:18, Migne 19:18, Catena intertext at Luke 6:32-36, Matt 18:15-17, James 2:1-7); refKeys carry both spans. Migne's Lev 19:1-2, 19:15 and most of 19:16 are Origen/Hesychius incipit-excipit pointers ('etc., as far as'), so only 19:18 was usable. Wesley's Gospel notes on 22:37-39 are bare cross-references, so the love-command doors rest on Catena + Migne; Wesley carries the David's-Lord door. Psalm rows (90, 1) inform gravity/synthesis only.]
trap: The great commandment shrinks to a slogan — it's all about love — and love shrinks to niceness: a warm feeling toward God and a pleasant manner toward people, with heart, soul, and mind left mostly where they were. The other trap is to preach the first half and drop the second, so that the passage becomes ethics without Christ, and Jesus' own question about David's son is never asked.
hinge: Jesus answers the test by asking for everything — all the heart, all the soul, all the mind, and the neighbour as yourself — and then turns and asks a question of his own that no one can answer: how can David's son be David's Lord? The commandment no one has kept and the One no one can account for stand side by side, and the passage ends not in an answer but in silence.

doors.claim: God asks to be loved with the whole of us — heart, soul, mind — so that no part of life is left for some other final good to claim.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: You are commanded to love God "with all thy heart," that your whole thoughts — "with all thy soul," that your whole life — "with all thy mind," that your whole understanding — may be given to Him from whom you have that you give. Thus He has left no part of our life which may justly be unfilled of Him; but if aught else present itself for the soul's love, it should be absorbed into that channel in which the whole current of love runs.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God. With his first answer the Lord strikes the feigned conscience of the questioner. With thy whole heart. The integrity of faith is expressed. In the whole soul, perfect obedience is required. In the whole mind, perseverance is shown.

witnesses.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: "Thou shalt love," not 'fear,' for to love is more than to fear; to fear belongs to slaves, to love to sons; fear is in compulsion, love in freedom. God does not desire to be served servilely by men as a master, but to be loved as a father, for that He has given the spirit of adoption to men.

doors.say: God doesn't want a slice of you, or a servant's careful obedience. He wants to be loved the way a child loves a father — with all of it.
doors.do: Ask them to name the one channel of their life — a worry, an ambition, a love — that runs somewhere other than toward God, and to turn it back into the main current this week.

doors.claim: The second commandment is like the first because it is the same love: the neighbour bears God's image, and we love him for God's sake and toward God.

witnesses.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: But who loves man is as who loves God; for man is God's image, wherein God is loved, as a King is honoured in his statue. For this cause this commandment is said to be like the first.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: If a man love his neighbour, it follows therefrom that he loves God also; for it is the selfsame affection by which we love God, and by which we love our neighbour, save that we love God for Himself, but ourselves and our neighbour for God's sake.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: Whoso then rightly loves his neighbour, ought to endeavour with him that he also with his whole heart love God.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: Quotation of Leviticus 19:18: You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. — The second commandment quoted verbatim: 'Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself' (22:39).

doors.say: You can't love God and skip the person in front of you — that person is God's image. And you haven't loved your neighbour until you've wanted God for them too.
doors.do: Have them pick one hard-to-love neighbour, honour God's image in that person by one concrete act, and pray that this neighbour come to love God with a whole heart.

doors.claim: Jesus turns from the question about the law to the question about himself: the Christ is more than a son of David, he is the Lord at God's right hand, and everything turns on who he is.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: How doth David then by the Spirit — By inspiration, call him Lord? If he be merely the son (or descendant) of David? The Lord said to my Lord — This his dominion, to which David himself was subject, shows both the heavenly majesty of the king, and the nature of his kingdom. Sit thou on my right hand - That is, remain in the highest authority and power.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: To my Lord. Not according to that whereby he was born of him, but according to that whereby he always was of the Father.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: Christ is therefore called David's Lord, not in respect of His descent from him, but in respect of His eternal generation from the Father, wherein He was before His fleshly Father. And he calls Him Lord, not by a mere chance, nor of his own thought, but by the Holy Spirit.

witnesses.author: Origen
witnesses.reading: For God puts Christ's enemies as a footstool beneath His feet, for their salvation as well as their destruction.

doors.say: The Pharisees came to test Jesus about the law. He sent them home with a harder question: who is this standing in front of you? The commandments are answered by the Lord who sits at God's right hand.
doors.do: Invite them to answer Jesus' question for themselves — not 'whose son is he?' in the abstract, but 'whose Lord is he?' — and to name one place in their week where they will live under his reign.

doors.claim: Israel's holiness is not a private piety but a likeness: the people are to be what their God is, and Jesus reads that likeness as mercy.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Be ye holy — Separated from all the forementioned defilements, and entirely consecrated to God and obedient to all his laws. I am holy - Both in my essence, and in all my laws, which are holy and just and good.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: 'Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful' is a deliberate reworking of the Holiness Code's imitatio Dei formula 'be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy.' The imitation-of-God structure is unmistakable; Luke substitutes mercy for holiness. (taken up at Luke 6:32-36)

doors.say: Holiness isn't keeping yourself clean from other people. It's looking like God among them — and God, Jesus says, looks like mercy.
doors.do: Ask them where in their week they can be like God in one particular — fair, truthful, merciful — on purpose, because he is.

doors.claim: Leviticus forbids the quiet grudge: to say nothing and nurse it is a form of hatred, and love tells the brother his fault for his good, not for the pleasure of being right.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Thou shalt not hate — As thou dost, in effect, if thou dost not rebuke him. If thy brother hath done wrong, thou shalt neither divulge it to others, nor hate him, and smother that hatred by sullen silence; nor flatter him therein, but shalt freely and in love, tell him of his fault.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Seek not revenge. That is, be not carried away by the lust of avenging while thou reprovest, so as to wish to rejoice or to be consoled at another's evil, but rather to take counsel for him whom thou reprovest. For thus has anger rightly been defined, as that which is the lust of avenging.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: 'Go, show him his fault between you and him alone' enacts the Holiness Code command 'you shall surely reprove your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him' — private, loving rebuke that does not let sin fester into hatred. (taken up at Matthew 18:15-17)

doors.say: Sullen silence feels like peace, but Leviticus calls it hate. Love goes and speaks — gently, privately, for the other person's sake.
doors.do: Have them name the one grievance they've been smothering, and either take it to that person in love this week or lay it down for good.

doors.claim: Neighbour-love begins in the courtroom: no tilting judgment toward the poor or the great, and no shrinking 'neighbour' to the people we already like.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: The poor — So as through pity to him to give an unrighteous sentence. Thy neighbour — Every man, as plainly appears, by comparing this place with ver. 34, where this law is applied to strangers. As thyself - With the same sincerity, though not equality of affection.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Thou shalt not stand against. As if to say, thou shalt not join thyself to those who lie in wait for their neighbours, as many do who, being allied with others, do what by themselves they cannot.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: James condemns showing partiality in the assembly. Leviticus 19:15 is the foundational prohibition: 'you shall not be partial to the poor or defer to the great, but in righteousness shall you judge your neighbor.' (taken up at James 2:1-7)

doors.say: God's law won't let you rig the scales — not for the powerful, and not even for the people you feel sorry for. Your neighbour is every person, including the one you'd rather leave out.
doors.do: Ask them to notice one place they take sides by habit — in a family quarrel, an online pile-on, a workplace faction — and to refuse to join the crowd against a neighbour.

complementary.gravity: God tells Israel to be holy because he is holy, and then spells holiness out in plain, unglamorous terms: judge without partiality, do not slander, do not stand against your neighbour's life, do not hate your brother in your heart but rebuke him, take no vengeance, bear no grudge, love your neighbour as yourself (Leviticus 19). The Psalm blesses the one whose delight is in that law day and night, rooted like a tree by water (Psalm 1). Paul reminds the Thessalonians he came among them gentle as a nurse, sharing not only the gospel but his own self; and Jesus, tested on the greatest commandment, quotes Leviticus as the second and says all the law hangs on the two. The nerve: holiness is the love of God made concrete toward the neighbour, and the law is not a ladder but a portrait of the God we are to resemble.

synthesis.convergence: Leviticus sets 'love your neighbour as yourself' at the end of a list of courtroom fairness, honest speech, and grudges refused, grounded in 'I am holy' (Leviticus 19); the Psalm finds the blessed life in delighting in that law (Psalm 1); Paul shows what it looks like in an apostle who gives himself, gently, to those he serves (1 Thessalonians 2); and Jesus names it the second great commandment, like the first (Matthew 22). Each reading makes love of God and love of neighbour one holiness, lived in particulars.
synthesis.claim: Be holy as God is holy — which means loving him with everything and loving your neighbour as yourself, in the courtroom, in your speech, and in the grudges you refuse to keep.
synthesis.here: For people who hear 'love your neighbour' as a warm sentiment they already agree with, the move is to let Leviticus make it specific — no favourites, no slander, no smothered resentment — and to find in Jesus' summary not a softening of the law but its heart.

doors.claim: Moses sees the whole promise and does not enter it; he dies in faith, and the seeing is itself a gift — the way believers see the promise before they possess it.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: He saw it at a distance. Such a sight the Old Testament believers had of the kingdom of the Messiah. And such a sight believers have now of the glory that shall he revealed. Those that come after us shall undoubtedly enter into that promised land: which is a comfort to us, when we find our own carcases falling in this wilderness.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Moses as well as the other fathers of the Old Testament, lifted up in spirit to the height of contemplation, were able to foresee the grace of the New Testament, which is given in Christ: but they could not await it in the flesh, and died in faith and hope.

doors.say: Moses got to see it all and not set foot in it. That's not a failure; it's how faith lives — seeing the promise from the mountain, and trusting those who come after to walk in.
doors.do: Ask them to name a promise or a work they may not live to see finished, and to give thanks for it from the mountain instead of grieving it from the valley.

doors.claim: The greatest servant of the Lord still dies; he climbs the mountain to meet it, God himself buries him, and the people are right to weep.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: When he knew the place of his death he cheerfully mounted a steep hill to come to it. Those who are well acquainted with another world, are not afraid to leave this. When God's servants are sent for out of the world, the summons runs go up and die!

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Neither his piety nor his usefulness would exempt him from the stroke of death. God's servants must die, that they may rest from their labours, receive their recompense, and make room for others. But when they go hence, they go to serve him better. The Jews say, God sucked his soul out of his body with a kiss. No doubt he died in the embraces of his love.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: And they wept. Because death reigned even in those who had not sinned, from Adam unto Moses: therefore tears follow him as he goes down to the lower regions. And they were completed. From this the custom seems to have arisen, that for the faithful departed the offices of piety are discharged for thirty days.

doors.say: Even Moses doesn't get to skip the ending. But he goes up the mountain to meet it, and God is there — and Israel still weeps for thirty days, because grief is a debt of love.
doors.do: Have them remember by name one servant of God they have lost, give thanks for that life, and let themselves grieve it honestly before God.

doors.claim: Deuteronomy closes by saying no prophet ever rose like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face; the church reads that as a door left open for the one greater than Moses.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Moses was greater than any other of the prophets of the Old Testament. But as far as the other prophets came short of him, our Lord Jesus went beyond him. Moses was faithful as a servant, but Christ as a son. Moses lies buried: but Christ is sitting at the right-hand of God, and of the increase of his government there shall be no end.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: And there arose not a prophet. Because Moses was more excellent than all the prophets of the Old Testament. But after the Lord of the prophets came incarnate into the world, all that former dignity and shadow of things to come ceased: because the law and the figure was given by Moses: grace and truth by Jesus Christ.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: 'No prophet has arisen since like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face' reinforces the face-to-face idiom as the unique mode of unmediated knowledge of God. (taken up at 1 Corinthians 13:8-12)

doors.say: The Torah ends with an empty place: no one like Moses. And then one comes who is not buried in an unknown valley but seated at God's right hand.
doors.do: Ask them to put their trust this week not in the great leaders who must die but in the Son who reigns — and to name one burden they will carry to him rather than to any Moses.

semicontinuous.gravity: Moses climbs Nebo, is shown the whole land from Gilead to the western sea, and is told he will not cross over; he dies there at the word of the Lord, God buries him where no one knows, Israel weeps thirty days, Joshua takes up the work, and the Torah closes saying no prophet has arisen like him, whom the Lord knew face to face (Deuteronomy 34). The Psalm is Moses' own prayer — Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations; our days are grass; satisfy us in the morning with your mercy, and establish the work of our hands (Psalm 90). Paul recalls giving his very self to the Thessalonians; and Jesus, after naming the two great commandments, asks how David's son can be David's Lord. The nerve: the greatest servant does not finish the journey, and every work of our hands is handed on — the one who finishes it is the Lord at God's right hand.

synthesis.convergence: Moses sees the promise and dies short of it, buried by God and mourned by Israel, with no prophet like him after (Deuteronomy 34); his prayer asks the everlasting God, our dwelling place, to make the work of brief lives last (Psalm 90); Paul pours out not only the gospel but himself for a church he will soon leave (1 Thessalonians 2); and Jesus points beyond David to David's Lord, seated at God's right hand (Matthew 22). Each reading sets a faithful servant's limits against a Lord who does not die and whose work does not end.
synthesis.claim: No servant of God finishes the journey — not even Moses — but the Lord who is our dwelling place establishes the work of our hands, and the Son reigns where Moses could not go.
synthesis.here: For a congregation that has buried faithful people, or is watching its own strength and years run short, the move is to stand with Moses on the mountain: see the promise, hand on the work, grieve honestly, and trust the One greater than Moses to bring it in.

subtract: These three are doors, not points — mutually exclusive landings (the whole self given to God / the neighbour loved as God's image / the question of who Jesus is). Walk through one and let the other two go; the choosing is the sermon's focus.
source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain), Wesley's Explanatory Notes, the Glossa ordinaria (Migne recension, Wroot Press English), and the Catena intertextual notes, retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.
